content: Buruli ulcer is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, a bacterium belonging to the same family as those responsible for tuberculosis and leprosy. The infection initially manifests as painless swelling, which later progresses to the development of skin lesions. As the disease advances, the bacteria produce toxins that suppress the immune system and lead to the destruction of skin, underlying tissues, and even bone. This can result in severe deformities. The disease primarily affects the limbs. The first description of Buruli ulcer was documented in 1948 in the Bairnsdale district of southeastern Australia. The pathophysiology of Buruli ulcer involves infection by Mycobacterium ulcerans. The disease begins with painless swelling, and over time, lesions form on the skin. The diagnosis of Buruli ulcer is typically based on the characteristic appearance of the ulcer in regions where the disease is endemic. When the diagnosis is uncertain, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing targeting the IS2404 sequence can be useful, although this test is not specific to Mycobacterium ulcerans. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain has a sensitivity of 40–80%, while culture methods have a sensitivity of 20–60%. Antibiotics play a limited role in the treatment of Buruli ulcer. The recommended antibiotics include rifampin, streptomycin, and dapsone. The primary treatment for Buruli ulcer is surgical excision of the lesion. If the disease is detected early, the surgery may be minor and highly effective. However, in advanced cases, treatment may require prolonged interventions, including extensive skin grafting. Surgical treatment can be challenging in resource-limited settings, where access to skilled surgical care is often scarce.
